#### Re-cap on whats explored

##### Data & pipeline

192 samples, 16,878 filtered gene targets, modeled with per-gene negative-binomial mixed models (glmmTMB) via the seqwrap/empirical-Bayes-shrinkage workflow (m1 naive → m2 regularized).
Fixed a sample-mapping error (one participant's t1 sample mislabeled as t2), which turned out to mean the study only has two real timepoints (t1 baseline, t3 follow-up) — the whole model, contrast set, and priors were rebuilt around a 3-level tx (baseline/t3low/t3mod) instead of the original assumed 5-level version.

Seqwrap package update mid-analysis — this changed some internal object structure (@summaries went from a list to a single combined data frame; @errors moved to a tidy long format) but did not change the underlying statistical output, confirmed by re-running the training-effect GSEA and comparing against pre-update results (matched almost exactly, differences only at permutation-noise level).

All contrasts updated to properly aggregate over sex (previously implicitly fixed at the modal sex level, since sex wasn't included in the datagrid() used for contrasts). Validated by hand-calculating two contrasts against the raw prediction grid. Empirical result: aggregating over sex made no material difference to any training-effect or volume-effect finding — gene counts, effect sizes, and GSEA top-hit tables all matched the non-aggregated version essentially exactly, suggesting sex was well-balanced across age×tx groups in this cohort. Kept as the methodologically correct approach regardless.

#### Baseline age differences (Young vs. Old, at t1)

- Marked transcriptional differences between age groups at baseline.
  - Young higher: aerobic energy metabolism — oxidative phosphorylation, mitochondrial gene expression.
  - Old higher: immune activation (humoral immune response, complement activation) and epigenetic/RNA regulation (heterochromatin formation, alternative mRNA splicing).
- Two originally-cited categories (foam cell differentiation, DNA replication) didn't survive the corrected data. Replaced in the write-up (see Results) with complement activation and heterochromatin formation — flagged for Daniel's review.

#### Training effect (baseline → t3), both age groups

Large, broad response in both young (3,503 genes) and old (4,241 genes) at FDR<5% — training clearly changes gene expression substantially. Unchanged after sex-aggregation. Remarkably similar biology between age groups — 6 of top 10 GO terms shared by exact ID (RNA splicing, ribonucleoprotein complex biogenesis, integrin-mediated signaling pathway, cell adhesion mediated by integrin, collagen metabolic process, mRNA transport), same direction/magnitude — consistent with the age×time interaction being essentially null at the gene level. Both groups' #1 hit is also a collagen/ECM-organization term (young: extracellular matrix organization; old: collagen fibril organization) — closely related, functionally overlapping, though not an exact ID match.

Pattern:
- Training up-regulates ECM/connective tissue remodeling (collagen metabolic process, integrin signaling/adhesion, ECM/collagen fibril organization)
- Training down-regulates RNA-processing/ribosome-biogenesis machinery (RNA splicing, ribonucleoprotein complex biogenesis, mRNA transport)

Non-shared categories: 
- Young-only: cytoplasmic translation, mesenchymal cell migration, angiogenesis; 
- Old-only: regulation of coagulation, cellular extravasation, regulation of blood coagulation. 
Young leans collagen/migration/angiogenesis, old leans coagulation/vascular — secondary difference, not contradictory to the main story.

Age × time interaction (young_old_t3): only 1 gene at FDR<5%, but GSEA on the same contrast shows a real, modest pathway-level signal (RNA splicing/mRNA processing shifts more in young; angiogenesis and aerobic respiration shift more in young). Diffuse, coordinated shift rather than individual standout genes.

#### Volume effect (Mod vs. Low), old adults only

- Young: essentially null (young_volume_t3, 1 gene) — no comparable volume effect.
- Old: weak but real signal (1,216 genes at FDR<5%) — moderate vs. low volume produces a detectable transcriptional difference.  
- The formal young-vs-old comparison of the volume effect (young_old_volume_t3) is null (0 genes), so "detectable in old but not in young" is the safe wording, not "present in old and absent in young". Unchanged after sex-aggregation.

Higher volume in old yielded more mitochondrial/oxidative signal (inner mitochondrial membrane organization, respiratory electron transport chain, purine-containing compound biosynthesis) but less muscle-contractile/translational signal (skeletal muscle contraction, cytoplasmic translation, muscle organ development, striated muscle cell differentiation, ribosomal small subunit biogenesis).
old_volume_t3's p.adjust values markedly weaker than the training-effect contrasts — real but modest signal (1,216 genes vs. 3,500–4,200 for the main training effects).

```{r}
#| code-fold: true


# Packages
library(reliefdata)
library(seqwrap)
library(tidyverse)
library(edgeR)
library(marginaleffects)
library(gt)
library(clusterProfiler)
library(org.Hs.eg.db)
library(AnnotationDbi)
library(english)

```


```{r}
#| code-fold: true
# Participants / samples -- Metadata
metadata <- reliefdata::relief_seqsamples |> 
  mutate(participant = as.character(participant)) |> 
  dplyr::rename(sample_weight = weight) |> 
  inner_join(relief_participants ) |> 
  inner_join(relief_volume |> 
               dplyr::select(-arm) |> 
              mutate(participant = as.character(participant)) ) |> 
  dplyr::select(participant, time, age, leg,sex, condition, allocation, sample_weight, seq_sample_id) |> 
  mutate(age = if_else(age < 40, "young", "old")) |> 
  arrange(seq_sample_id)

metadata <- metadata |>
  mutate(time = if_else(
    participant == "3003" & time == "t2" & leg == "L" & condition == "mod",
    "t1",
    time
  )) # t1 L sample wrongfully labelled as t2 for this participant, this fixes it short-term, but it should be looked into closer. 



# Read gene-level data 
dat <- readRDS("data-raw-rnaseq/relief_gene.RDS"); dat <- dat$expected_count


# Number of samples to RNA-seq
nsamp <- stringr::str_to_sentence(as.english(nrow(metadata)))
nsamp_included <- (ncol(dat) - 1)

saveRDS(
  list(n_selected = nrow(metadata),       # samples selected for sequencing
       n_included = ncol(dat) - 1),       # samples passing QC (RIN > 8)
  "data-out/rnaseq-sample-counts.RDS"
)

```


`r nsamp` total RNA samples were selected for RNA-sequencing analysis of which `r nsamp_included` samples passed initial quality assessment (RIN > 8) and were used in downstream analyses. Purified mRNA (poly-T oligo-attached magnetic beads) was used for library preparation and subsequent 150-bp paired-end sequencing (Illumina NovaSeq, Novogene Europe, Cambridge, United Kingdom). Raw reads were filtered (SOFTWARE, settings) and aligned to the Human genome (Release) followed by gene and transcript level quantification using RSEM (version).

Gene counts (filtered for low-abundance targets) were modeled using a regularized negative binomial generalized linear mixed model [@glmmmtb] including model parameters for sex, time (baseline, week 3 and week 12), age-group (young and old) and condition (low- and moderate-volume) and the interaction between time age and condition. A varying intercept (random effect) was used for participant, and the dispersion parameter was estimated using the `nbinom2` parameterization available in `glmmTMB`[@glmmmtb]. The effective library size [@robinson2010;@edger] was included as an offset to account for sequencing depth. Regularization through an empirical Bayes shrinkage approach[@efron2010] was achieved using a two-step approach. First, naive models were fitted for all target counts (gene/transcript) using our in-house pipeline [@seqwrap] and estimates for all model parameters (except the intercept) were used to create priors for subsequent informed models. Fixed effect priors were constructed using a normal distribution with mean and standard deviations from each parameter value from the first model pass, the prior for the varying intercepts were constructed using a gamma distribution with the shape parameter informed by the mean from the naive model estimates and the  scale parameter fixed to 2. Finally, the dispersion parameter priors were constructed by fitting a trend model (Local Polynomial Regression Fit) to the association between raw mean log counts and log dispersion across all targets. The predicted dispersion at target-specific raw mean log count was used as the mean and the model residual standard error was used as the standard deviation to define a normally distributed target-specific prior.

```{r}
#| include: false

# Plot samples

metadata |> 
  dplyr::select(participant, time, age, allocation, condition) |> 
  mutate(obs = "obs") |> 
  pivot_wider(names_from = time, 
              values_from = obs) |> 
  arrange(participant) |> 
  pivot_longer(names_to = "time",
               values_to = "obs", 
               cols = t3:t1 ) |> 
  ggplot(aes(time, participant, 
             fill = obs)) + geom_point(shape = 21) +
  facet_wrap(age ~ condition, scales = "free_y")



metadata |> 
  summarise(.by = c(time, age, condition), 
            n = n()) |> 
  arrange(time)





```


Before fitting preliminary models to gene count data, the count matrix is filtered for low-abundance genes using `edgeR::filterByExpr` using sex and age as the grouping variable. The count matrix is used to calculate the trimmed mean of M values approach (TMM) [@robinson2010;@edger]. 


```{r}
#| code-fold: true

# Confirm sample names in seq_sample_id,
# all(colnames(dat[,-1]) %in% metadata$seq_sample_id)

# All samples in the data exists in the meta data
# all(metadata$seq_sample_id %in% colnames(dat[,-1]))
# Not all sample id's are in the data

# Subset the metadata to match the data
metadata <- metadata |> 
  filter(seq_sample_id %in% colnames(dat[,-1]))


# Sort the data 
# all_of provides a fail safe as it checks that all samples are 
# in the data
dat <- dat |> 
  dplyr::select(gene_id, all_of(metadata$seq_sample_id)) 


# Filter by expression
keep <- filterByExpr(
    dat[,-1],
    min.count = 10,
    min.total.count = 15,
    large.n = 10,
    min.prop = 0.7,
    group = paste(metadata$sex, metadata$age))

# Convert to DGE list for library size normalization
dat_filtered <- dat[keep,] |> 
  mutate(across(starts_with("R"), as.integer)) |> 
  data.frame()

y <- DGEList(dat_filtered[,-1])
y <- normLibSizes(y, method = "TMM")

# Get CPM-values for downstream analyses
logcpm_y <- cpm(y, log = TRUE, prior.count = 2)



libSize <- y$samples |> 
  rownames_to_column(var = "seq_sample_id") |>
    dplyr::select(-group)


metadata2 <- metadata |> 
  inner_join(libSize) |> 
  mutate(efflibsize = (lib.size * norm.factors) / median(lib.size * norm.factors), 
         ln_efflibsize = log(efflibsize), 
         tx = if_else(time == "t1", "baseline", paste0(time, condition)), 
         tx = factor(tx, levels = c("baseline", "t3low", "t3mod")), 
         age = factor(age, levels = c("old", "young")), 
         sex = factor(sex, levels = c("male", "female"))) |> 
  dplyr::select(-lib.size, -norm.factors) 


```


## Model prototyping

We are constructing a model that will capture:

- Effects of the training intervention averaged over age and volume conditions (descriptive)
- Average effects of the training intervention within age groups, averaged over volume conditions (descriptive)
- Differences between age groups in change from baseline to time 3, averaged over volume conditions (inferential)
- Differences between volume conditions at time 3, averaged over age groups (inferential) 
- Differences between volume conditions at time 3 within age groups (descriptive)
- Differences between volume conditions between age groups at time 3 (inferential)

We separate descriptive from inferential contrasts here to avoid making claims about, e.g., age-group differences based on informal comparisons of within-group effects without a formal contrast. The within-group contrasts can still be used for description. Sex is added as a control variable to balance any sex differences between groups and time points.

The model can be described as 

$$
\begin{align}
y_{i[g]} &\sim \operatorname{NB2}(\mu_{i[g]}, \phi_{[g]}) \\
\log(\mu_{i[g]} ) &= \beta_{k[g]}X_i  + \log(S_i) + b_{0i[g]} \\
\beta_{k[g]}X_i &= \beta_{0[g]} + \beta_{1[g]}\text{Sex}_i + \beta_{2[g]}\text{A}_i + \beta_{3[g]}\text{TX1}_i + \beta_{4[g]}\text{TX2}_i + \beta_{5[g]}(\text{A}_i \times \text{TX1}_i) + \beta_{6[g]}(\text{A}_i \times \text{TX2}_i)\\ 
b_{0i[g]} &\sim \operatorname{Normal}(0, \sigma_{b[g]}) \\
\end{align}
$$
where the gene expression levels for gene *g*, and row *i* in the meta data ($y_{i[g]}$), is distributed according to a negative binomial distribution with mean $\mu_{i[g]}$ and dispersion $\phi_{[g]}$. The linear predictor for $\mu_{i[g]}$ has a set of fixed effects $\beta_{k[g]}X_i$, an offset term $\log(S_i)$ describing the TMM normalized library size as a fraction of the median library size, and a participant-level varying intercept ($b_{0i[g]}$). The fixed effects contain parameters describing the intercept ($\beta_{0[g]}$) representing the expression level in male participants in the old age-group at baseline (`time == "t1"`), the difference between sexes ($\beta_{1[g]}\text{Sex}_i$, female vs. male), the difference between age groups (*A*, young vs. old) at baseline ($\beta_{2[g]}\text{A}_i$), the time-condition effects in the reference level age group (old), $\beta_{3[g]}\text{TX1}_i$ and $\beta_{4[g]}\text{TX2}_i$, and the interactions between age and the time-condition effects, $\beta_{5[g]}(\text{A}_i \times \text{TX1}_i)$ and $\beta_{6[g]}(\text{A}_i \times \text{TX2}_i)$. The time-condition factor (`tx`) has three levels: baseline (all participants at `t1`, the reference), time 3 after low-volume training (TX1, `t3low`) and time 3 after moderate-volume training (TX2, `t3mod`). It thus combines time-point and volume condition (low vs. moderate volume). In the fitted model objects these parameters are named `(Intercept)`, `sexfemale`, `ageyoung`, `txt3low`, `txt3mod`, `ageyoung:txt3low` and `ageyoung:txt3mod`, in addition to the participant standard deviation (`sd__(Intercept)`).

\beta_{k[g]}X_i &= \beta_{0[g]} + \beta_{1[g]}\text{Sex}_i + \beta_{2[g]}\text{A}_i + \beta_{3[g]}\text{TX1}_i + \beta_{4[g]}\text{TX2}_i + \beta_{5[g]}\text{TX3}_i + \beta_{6[g]}\text{TX4}_i + \beta_{7[g]}(\text{A}_i \times \text{TX1}_i) + \beta_{8[g]}(\text{A}_i \times \text{TX2}_i) + \beta_{9[g]}(\text{A}_i \times \text{TX3}_i)+ \beta_{10[g]}(\text{A}_i \times \text{TX4}_i)\\

We will use `glmmTMB` to fit the model using the `nbinom2` family function. The dispersion ($\phi$) parameter will be part of describing the variance in the model as $\operatorname{Var}(y_i) = \mu_i + \frac{\mu^2_i}{\phi}$. A large $\phi$ indicate that overdispersion in relation to a Poisson dispersion is small, as $\phi$ decrease, over-dispersion increase[^notes-on-parameterization]. 

[^notes-on-parameterization]: See `?glmmTMB::nbinom2` for a description of the dispersion parameterization. We have previously used the same parameterization in describing the seqwrap[@seqwrap]. 

Using this model we can construct the custom contrasts needed to get estimates of the comparisons listed above. Contrasts are created using the `marginaleffects` package[@marginaleffects] and incorporated in the in the seqwrap workflow as outlined below.

First we fit prototype model to a subset of the data set (a subset of gene targets). 

```{r}
# Set up the model prototype in seqwrap_compose
m0 <- seqwrap_compose(
  modelfun = glmmTMB::glmmTMB, 
  # Using alist to avoid evaluation of list components
  arguments = alist(
    # The model formula and family function needs to be explicitly
    # referenced here. 
    formula = y ~ sex + age * tx + offset(ln_efflibsize) + (1|participant), 
    family = glmmTMB::nbinom2()
    ),
  # Data, metadata and sample id
  data = dat_filtered, 
  metadata = metadata2, 
  samplename = "seq_sample_id")

m0r <- seqwrap(m0, 
        cores = 12,
        # Using a subset will give us 12 models to experiment on
        subset = 1:12, 
        # return_models will save models in the result object 
        return_models = TRUE)
```

The prototyping worked without any error or warning messages. Next we extract one model to build the contrast around. @tbl-model-prototype-tidy shows estimates from the initial model. 

```{r}
#| label: tbl-model-prototype-tidy
# Extract a model object
m <- m0r@models[[1]]


broom.mixed::tidy(m) |> 
  gt() |> 
  fmt_auto()
```

Using `predictions` from the `marginaleffects` package we can extract predictions at a specified data grid. The data grid specified in the code below will give us predictions at combinations of age and `tx` (the combination of volume condition and time) at an offset of 0 (the median library size). The resulting predictions are shown in @tbl-model-prototype-predictions

```{r}
#| label: tbl-model-prototype-predictions

marginaleffects::predictions(m, 
                                   re.form = NA,
                                   type = "link",
                                   newdata = datagrid(tx = unique, 
                                                      age = unique, 
                                                      ln_efflibsize = 0)) |> 
  data.frame() |> 
  dplyr::select(rowid, age, tx, ln_efflibsize, estimate) |> 
  gt() |> 
  fmt_auto()


```

The next step is to set up contrasts. This can be done using the hypothesis argument in `marginaleffects::predictions`. As a sanity check we add a single contrast, with a corresponding single parameter value in the model output (@tbl-model-prototype-prediction-contrast). This contrast corresponds to the parameter `ageyoung` in the model summary (@tbl-model-prototype-prediction-modelsummary).

<!-- NOTE (KL): this prototype chunk uses the 6-row datagrid WITHOUT sex (b1 = old/baseline, b2 = young/baseline). The final sum_fun_contr further down uses the 12-row datagrid WITH sex, where b1-b12 map differently. Both are correct for what they do; this chunk is kept as the simple sanity check. -->

```{r}
#| label: tbl-model-prototype-prediction-contrast

marginaleffects::predictions(m, 
                                   re.form = NA,
                                   type = "link",
                                   newdata = datagrid(tx = unique, 
                                                      age = unique, 
                                                      ln_efflibsize = 0),
                                   hypothesis = c(
                                     # This contrast is the same as ageyoung in the model summary
                                     "young_old_baseline" = "b2 - b1 = 0")) |> 
   data.frame() |> 
  gt() |> 
  fmt_auto()


```


```{r}
#| label: tbl-model-prototype-prediction-modelsummary

broom.mixed::tidy(m) |> 
  filter(term == "ageyoung") |> 
  gt() |> 
  fmt_auto()


```

We are now building a full function that takes a model object as its input and returns a data frame with contrast estimates. We also include the parameter estimates for downstream analyses. Note that the marginaleffects package will return a warning when specifying custom contrasts for the first time in a sessions. Since seqwrap will initialize a new session for each target we need to disable this warning (`options(marginaleffects_safe = FALSE)`) to avoid polluting our summary slot. The function `sum_fun_contr` can be tested on a single model object before being included as part of a seqwrap model object. @tbl-model-testsumfun shows the output from the custom summary function.  

```{r}
#| label: tbl-model-testsumfun

## Contrasts averaged over sex: sex is included in the datagrid (12 rows:
## 3 tx x 2 age x 2 sex) and every hypothesis averages over both sex levels.
## Row order (verified): b1 old/male/baseline, b2 old/female/baseline,
## b3 young/male/baseline, b4 young/female/baseline, b5 old/male/t3low,
## b6 old/female/t3low, b7 young/male/t3low, b8 young/female/t3low,
## b9 old/male/t3mod, b10 old/female/t3mod, b11 young/male/t3mod,
## b12 young/female/t3mod.

sum_fun_contr <- function(m) {
  
  options(marginaleffects_safe = FALSE)
  
  est <- broom.mixed::tidy(m)
  
  terms <- est |> 
    dplyr::pull(term)
  
  checkterms <- c("(Intercept)", 
                  "sexfemale", 
                  "ageyoung", 
                  "txt3low", 
                  "txt3mod",
                  "ageyoung:txt3low", 
                  "ageyoung:txt3mod",
                  "sd__(Intercept)")
  
  if(!all(terms == checkterms)) stop("The terms are different from expected, contrasts may not be correct. Check the contrasts and model formulation.")

  contrasts <- marginaleffects::predictions(m, 
                                   re.form = NA,
                                   type = "link",
                                   newdata = marginaleffects::datagrid(
                                     tx = unique, 
                                     age = unique, 
                                     sex = unique,          # <-- ADDED
                                     ln_efflibsize = 0),
                                   hypothesis = c(
                                     "young_old_baseline" = "((b3+b4)/2) - ((b1+b2)/2) = 0",
                                     "young_t3" = "(((b7+b8)/2) + ((b11+b12)/2))/2 - ((b3+b4)/2) = 0",
                                     "old_t3"   = "(((b5+b6)/2) + ((b9+b10)/2))/2 - ((b1+b2)/2) = 0",
                                     "young_old_t3" = "((((b7+b8)/2) + ((b11+b12)/2))/2 - ((b3+b4)/2)) - ((((b5+b6)/2) + ((b9+b10)/2))/2 - ((b1+b2)/2)) = 0",
                                     "mod_low_t3" = "((((b9+b10)/2) + ((b11+b12)/2))/2) - ((((b5+b6)/2) + ((b7+b8)/2))/2) = 0",
                                     "young_volume_t3" = "((b11+b12)/2) - ((b7+b8)/2) = 0",
                                     "old_volume_t3"   = "((b9+b10)/2) - ((b5+b6)/2) = 0",
                                     "young_old_volume_t3" = "(((b11+b12)/2) - ((b7+b8)/2)) - (((b9+b10)/2) - ((b5+b6)/2)) = 0"
                                     ))
  
  out <- contrasts |> 
    data.frame() |> 
    dplyr::mutate(effect = "contrast", 
           component = "contrast", 
           group = NA) |> 
    dplyr::select(term = hypothesis, effect, component, group, estimate:p.value, conf.low, conf.high ) |> 
    dplyr::bind_rows(
      est |> 
    dplyr::mutate(conf.low = NA, 
           conf.high = NA) |> 
    dplyr::select(term, effect, component, group, estimate:p.value, conf.low, conf.high)
    )
  
  return(out)
}

#    dplyr::mutate(conf.low = NA, 
#           conf.high = NA) |> 
#    dplyr::select(term, effect, component, group, estimate:p.value, conf.low, conf.high)
#    )
#  
#  # Bind with model estimates
#  
#  return(out)
#}


sum_fun_contr(m) |> 
  gt() |> 
  fmt_auto()

```

For the next step in the workflow we will need to extract estimates of the dispersion parameter. We will use the evaluation slot in `seqwrap` to do this. We will borrow code from the [`seqwrappaper`](https://github.com/trainome/seqwrappaper) allowing us to expand the model later to a Poisson observation-level random effect model. The custom evaluation function will give us an estimate of $\phi$ (dispersion) and convergence statistics. The evaluation function is built below and tested on a model object. 


```{r}
#| label: tbl-model-testevalfun

# Summary function for seqwrap
sigma_summary2 <- function(x) {
  if (is.null(x$fit$convergence)) {
    conv <- 1
  } else {
    conv <- x$fit$convergence[[1]]
  }
  ### Simulating scaled resid ###
  # This creates simulated residuals for test of uniformity and dispersion.
  # See
  # https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/DHARMa/vignettes/DHARMa.html
  # for details.
  residObj <- DHARMa::simulateResiduals(x, plot = FALSE)

  # Saving tests from DHARMa
  unif <- DHARMa::testUniformity(residObj, plot = FALSE)
  disp <- DHARMa::testDispersion(residObj, plot = FALSE)

  # Saving SD of Obs Level Rand Eff in the Poisson model

  tidy_coef <- broom.mixed::tidy(x)

  if (any(tidy_coef$group %in% "seq_sample_id")) {
    olre.sd <- tidy_coef |>
      dplyr::filter(group == "seq_sample_id") |>
      dplyr::pull(estimate)
  } else {
    olre.sd <- NA
  }

  # Combine all in a data frame
  out <- data.frame(
    dispersion = data.frame(summary(x$sdr))["betadisp", 1],
    dispersion.se = data.frame(summary(x$sdr))["betadisp", 2],
    olre.sd = olre.sd,
    log_mu = mean(stats::predict(x, type = "link")),
    convergence = conv,
    pdHess = x$sdr$pdHess,
    aic = stats::AIC(x),
    unif.p = unif$p.value,
    unif.stat = unif$statistic,
    disp.p = disp$p.value,
    disp.stat = disp$statistic
  )
  return(out)
}


sigma_summary2(m)

```

We are ready to build the full model with custom summary functions.  

```{r}

# Set up the model prototype in seqwrap_compose
m1 <- seqwrap_compose(
  modelfun = glmmTMB::glmmTMB, 
  # Using alist to avoid evaluation of list components
  arguments = alist(
    # The model formula and family function needs to be explicitly
    # referenced here. 
    formula = y ~ sex + age * tx + offset(ln_efflibsize) + (1|participant), 
    family = glmmTMB::nbinom2()
    ),
  # Data, metadata and sample id
  eval_fun = sigma_summary2, 
  summary_fun = sum_fun_contr,
  data = dat_filtered, 
  metadata = metadata2, 
  samplename = "seq_sample_id")

m1r <- seqwrap(m1, 
        cores = 12,
        # Using a subset will give us 12 models to experiment on
        subset = 1:12, 
        # return_models will save models in the result object 
        return_models = TRUE)


```

The subset models turns out to give us both summaries and evaluations. We can proceed to model the full data set.

## Updating the model with empirical Bayes shrinkage

The preliminary estimates from the first pass of the data will serve as basis for shrinkage in a second pass. This procedure is a pragmatic empirical Bayes procedure that we apply to relevant parameters of the model to achieve regularization on more stable estimates [@seqwrap;@efron2010, pp 4-]. Using the raw mean counts as a predictor we fit a local polynomial regression to capture the trend of the dispersion estimates (@fig-dispersion-trend). The trend serves as the basis of a normal prior with the trend as the mean and the standard error as the standard deviation. 

```{r}
#| code-fold: true
#| label: fig-dispersion-trend
#| fig-cap: "A loess trend for the relationship between raw log-counts means and dispersion. Shaded regions represent 50, 95 and 99% quantile prediction intervals."


# Summarise estimates from the preliminary model
m1s <- seqwrap_summarise(m1r, verbose = FALSE)

# Collect all model parameter estimates  
eb_estimates <- m1s$summaries |> 
  filter(term %in% c("sexfemale", 
                     "ageyoung", 
                     "txt3low", 
                     "txt3mod", 
                     "ageyoung:txt3low", 
                     "ageyoung:txt3mod", 
                     "sd__(Intercept)")) |> 
  summarise(.by = term, 
             m = mean(estimate), 
             s = sd(estimate)) 
  


# Extract phi vs. raw counts
raw_mu <- data.frame(
  target = dat_filtered[,1],
  log_mu_raw = log(rowMeans(dat_filtered[,-1]))) 

# The dispersion data is combined here with raw counts means
dispersion_data <- m1s$evaluations |> 
  dplyr::select(target, dispersion, dispersion.se, log_mu) |> 
  inner_join(raw_mu) 


# Fit a loess model 
trend_model <- loess(dispersion ~ log_mu_raw, 
      data = dispersion_data, 
      span = 0.7)


# Predictions from the trend model. Here we use simulations to approximate 
# 50, 95 and 99% quantile intervals around the predicted mean to visualize the 
# implied shrinkage prior.

# Original (hardcoded range; predict.loess returns NA outside the range of the
# fitted data, which broke this step after the seqwrap update):
#pred <- data.frame(
#  log_mu_raw = seq(from = 1.5, to = 13.5, by = 0.1), 
#  disp_pred = predict(trend_model, newdata = data.frame(log_mu_raw = seq(from = 1.5, to = 13.5, by = 0.1)))
#) |>

# Changed: derive the prediction range from the data
mu_range <- range(dispersion_data$log_mu_raw, na.rm = TRUE)

pred <- data.frame(
  log_mu_raw = seq(from = mu_range[1], to = mu_range[2], by = 0.1), 
  disp_pred = predict(trend_model, 
                       newdata = data.frame(log_mu_raw = seq(from = mu_range[1], to = mu_range[2], by = 0.1)))
) |> 
  expand_grid(draw = 1:2000) |> 
  rowwise() |> 
  mutate(pred_int = rnorm(1, mean = disp_pred, sd = trend_model$s)) |> 
  ungroup() |> 
  summarise(.by = c(log_mu_raw, disp_pred), 
            lwr50 = quantile(pred_int, 0.25), 
            upr50 = quantile(pred_int, 0.75),
            lwr95 = quantile(pred_int, 0.025), 
            upr95 = quantile(pred_int, 0.975), 
            lwr99 = quantile(pred_int, 0.015), 
            upr99 = quantile(pred_int, 0.995)) 


dispersion_data |> 
  dplyr::select(target, dispersion, dispersion.se, log_mu) |> 
  inner_join(raw_mu) |> 
  ggplot(aes(log_mu_raw, dispersion)) + 
  geom_point(alpha = 0.2) +
  geom_line(data = pred, 
            aes(log_mu_raw, 
                disp_pred), 
            color = "blue", 
            linewidth = 1.5) + 
  geom_ribbon(data = pred, 
              aes(log_mu_raw, 
                disp_pred, 
                ymin = lwr50, 
                ymax =upr50), 
              alpha = 0.2) + 
  geom_ribbon(data = pred, 
              aes(log_mu_raw, 
                disp_pred, 
                ymin = lwr95 , 
                ymax = upr95), 
              alpha = 0.2) + 
  geom_ribbon(data = pred, 
              aes(log_mu_raw, 
                disp_pred, 
                ymin = lwr99, 
                ymax =upr99), 
              alpha = 0.2) +
  labs(x = "Mean raw counts (log)", 
       y = "Dispersion (log &phi;)") + 
  theme(axis.title.y = ggtext::element_markdown())


```


Similarly, for all fixed effects parameters, except the intercept, we use the mean and standard deviation of the preliminary estimates to create priors. For the varying intercepts (`sd__(Intercept)`) we will use a gamma distribution to weakly regularize this parameter. The intercept parameter will be left without a prior as it is on different scales depending on the gene target. 

The code below first extracts the trend model predictions for the dispersion estimate then combine these on a target-by-target basis with a overall fixed-effect estimates.


```{r}
#| code-fold: true


dispersion_prior <- data.frame(
  target = dat_filtered[,1], 
  pred = round(
    predict(
      trend_model,
      newdata = data.frame(log_mu_raw = log(rowMeans(dat_filtered[,-1])))),
    3),
  s = round(trend_model$s, 3)) |>
 mutate(prior = paste0("normal(", pred, ",", s, ")")) 
  


# Guard: the class vector below is hard-coded to 6 fixef terms + 1 ranef term
stopifnot(nrow(eb_estimates) == 7)

fixef_priors <- eb_estimates |> 
  mutate(prior = if_else(term == "sd__(Intercept)", 
                         paste0("gamma(", 
                                round(m, 3), 
                                ",", 2, ")"), 
                         paste0("normal(", 
                        round(m, 3), 
                        ",", 
                        round(s, 3), ")")), 
         class = c(rep("fixef", 6), "ranef"), 
         coef = if_else(term == "sd__(Intercept)", "participant", term))   |> 
  dplyr::select(prior, class, coef)
  

Priors_list <- list() 
for(j in 1:nrow(dat_filtered)) {
  
  df <- bind_rows(
    fixef_priors, 
    data.frame(
      prior = dispersion_prior[dispersion_prior$target == dat_filtered[j,1],4], 
      class = "fixef_disp", 
      coef = "1") )
  
  Priors_list[[j]] <- df
  
}




```

We will now build the model with regularizing (empirical Bayes) priors. The test run (@tbl-regprior-example) confirms that the prior is part of the model.

```{r}
#| code-fold: true
#| label: tbl-regprior-example

m2 <-  seqwrap_compose(
  modelfun = glmmTMB::glmmTMB, 
  # Using alist to avoid evaluation of list components
  arguments = alist(
    # The model formula and family function needs to be explicitly
    # referenced here. 
    formula = y ~ sex + age * tx + offset(ln_efflibsize) + (1|participant), 
    family = glmmTMB::nbinom2(), 
    priors = data.frame(
      prior = prior, 
      class = class, 
      coef = coef)),
  # Data, metadata and sample id
  eval_fun = sigma_summary2, 
  summary_fun = sum_fun_contr,
  targetdata = Priors_list,
  data = dat_filtered, 
  metadata = metadata2, 
  samplename = "seq_sample_id")


m2r <- seqwrap(
  m2, 
  cores = 12, 
  subset = 1:12, 
  return_models = TRUE
)


m2r@models[[1]]$modelInfo$priors |> 
  gt()



```

#### Age-related differences at baseline

We first explore the age-related differences at baseline. Below we define two wrapper-functions to perform rank-based gene-set enrichment analysis using clusterProfiler [@xu2024a]. 

```{r}
#| code-fold: true

# Get all genes belonging to Gene Ontology gene sets to allow for finding diff
# genes not belonging to gene set.
 
 bp_genes <- AnnotationDbi::select(
  org.Hs.eg.db,
  keys    = keys(org.Hs.eg.db, keytype = "ENTREZID"),
  columns = "ONTOLOGY",
  keytype = "ENTREZID"
) |>
  subset(ONTOLOGY == "BP") |>
  _$ENTREZID |>
  unique()
 
 
 bp_genes <- bitr(bp_genes, "ENTREZID", "ENSEMBL", OrgDb = org.Hs.eg.db) |> 
   pull(ENSEMBL)
 
# A function to perform rank-based gene-set enrichment and find genes 
# not included in the gene sets that are FDR < 0.05.
#
#
# sums, a seqwrap summary table. 
# coef, the coefficient of interest
# setgenes, genes in the gene sets


 
 
gsea_fun <- function(sums, coef, setgenes, ontology = "BP") {
  
  

  # Create the statistics from the gene list
  gene_list <- sums |> 
    filter(term == coef )|>
    # Separate for ensemble and symbol
    separate_wider_regex(
    target,
    patterns = c(
      ensembl  = "ENSG\\d+",
      "\\.",
      version  = "[^_]+",      
      "_",
      symbol   = ".+"
    )
  ) |> 
    # Do FDR correction of the p-values
    mutate(p.value = p.adjust(p.value, method = "BH")) |> 
    # Arrange for the gsea
    arrange(desc(statistic)) |>      # Troubleshooting revealed this needs to be in descending order, thus adding desc() - seems like this might be a packageversion thing
    dplyr::select(symbol, ensembl, estimate, std.error, statistic, p.value) 
  
  # Compile gene list vector
  geneList <- gene_list$statistic
  names(geneList) <- as.character(gene_list$ensembl)
  

  # GSE ranked based
  gse_res <- gseGO(
    geneList = geneList,

    OrgDb = org.Hs.eg.db,
    ont = ontology,
    
   # method = "multilevel", # produces error, might stem from the same packageversion issue? Current fgsea/clusterProfiler defaults to the multilevel algorithm automatically for GSEA when eps = 0 (already in our call)
   
    keyType = "ENSEMBL",
    minGSSize = 25,
    maxGSSize = 500,
    pvalueCutoff = 0.01,
    nPermSimple = 10000,   # default is 1000
    eps         = 0,       # remove the lower bound on reported p-values
    verbose = FALSE
  )
  # Simplify the results
  gse_res2 <- simplify(gse_res, cutoff = 0.5, by = "NES", 
                       select_fun = function(x) x[which.max(abs(x))])
  
  data.frame(gse_res2) |> 
    dplyr::select(Description, p.adjust, NES) |> 
    arrange(p.adjust)
 
 # Subset the gene_list to only contain genes not in genesets
 # shortlisted on   
 diff_genes <- gene_list |> 
   filter(!(ensembl %in% setgenes )) |> 
   filter(p.value < 0.01) |> 
   arrange(-abs(estimate ))
 
 
 
 
 # Output
 out_list <- list(diff_genes_out = diff_genes, 
                  gene_list = gene_list,
                  gse_results_filtered = gse_res2, 
                  gse_results = gse_res)
 

 
}
  


# Function for plotting a enrichment score for specific gene sets
#
#
# NB: colscale needs length(genesets) + 1 colours (1 background + 1 per set).
gse_plot <- function(gseresults, genesets = c("GO:0042775", "GO:0000398"), 
                     colscale = c("gray80", "#DE8F05", "#009E73")) {
  
  
   # Get the running score
  
  pdat <- list()
  for(i in seq_along(genesets)) {
    
    temp_dat <- enrichplot::gseaplot(gseresults, geneSetID = genesets[i])
    pdat[[i]] <- temp_dat[[1]]$data
    
  }
  

   # Combine data set 
   dat <- bind_rows(pdat) |> 
     mutate(Description = stringr::str_to_sentence(Description), 
            Description = gsub("mrna", "mRNA", Description), 
            Description = fct_reorder(Description, runningScore, 
                                      .fun = max))
   
   
   p1 <- dat |> 
     ggplot(aes(x, runningScore)) + 
     geom_line(aes(color = Description)) +
     scale_color_manual(values = colscale[-1]) +
     theme_classic() + 
     theme(axis.text.x = element_blank(), 
           axis.title.x = element_blank(), 
           axis.ticks.x = element_blank(), 
           axis.line.x = element_blank(), 
           legend.title = element_blank(), 
           legend.position  = "top",
            legend.direction = "vertical", 
           legend.justification = "left") +
     labs(y = "Enrichment score") + 
     guides(color = guide_legend(reverse = TRUE))
     

  
  p2 <-  dat |> 
     ggplot(aes(x = x, xend = x, 
                y = 0, yend = geneList)) + 
     geom_segment(color = colscale[1]) + 

      geom_segment(data = filter(dat, 
                                position == 1), 
                  aes(color = Description))  +
     theme_classic() + 
    scale_color_manual(values = colscale[-1])  + 
    theme(legend.position = "none") + 
    labs(y = "Contrast effect size\n(z-score)", 
         x = "Gene rank position")
     
  
   p <- cowplot::plot_grid(p1, p2, align = "v", 
                     ncol = 1, 
                     rel_heights = c(1, 0.6))
  
  return(p) 
  
}
```

```{r}
cor_df <- data.frame( cor_mat) |> 
  mutate(target = ensembl) |> 
  dplyr::select(target, all_of(non_annotated)) 


gsea_annotate <- function(k, ontology = "BP") {
  
  gene_id <- colnames(cor_df)[1+k]
  
  dat <- cor_df[,c(1, 1 + k)]  |> 
    data.frame()
  
  gene_list <- dat |> 
    dplyr::rename(correlation = 2) |> 
#    arrange(-abs(correlation)) |> # sorts by absolute value, not actual, seemingly produced: simpleError condition: geneList should be a decreasing sorted vector..
    arrange(desc(correlation)) |> #should fix the error above
    filter(target != gene_id) 
  
   # Compile gene list vector
  geneList <- gene_list$correlation
  names(geneList) <- as.character(gene_list$target)
  

  # GSE ranked based
  gse_res <- gseGO(
    geneList = geneList,

    OrgDb = org.Hs.eg.db,
    ont = ontology,
    
    #method = "multilevel", # removed, same reason as in gsea_fun
    
    keyType = "ENSEMBL",
    minGSSize = 25,
    maxGSSize = 500,
    pvalueCutoff = 0.01,
    nPermSimple = 1000,   # default is 1000
    eps         = 0,       # remove the lower bound on reported p-values
    verbose = FALSE
  )
  
  gse_res <- gse_res |> 
    data.frame(row.names = NULL) |> 
    dplyr::select(ID, Description, setSize, NES, p.adjust) |> 
    arrange(-NES) |> 
    mutate(target = gene_id)
 
  return(gse_res)

  
}

})

# A function for clustering results from non-annotated genes
#
#
# gene, a list of non-annotated genes
# cor_df, the correlation data frame
cluster_fun <- function(genes, cor_df, go_annotation) {
  
  # This subsets the correlations data frame for rows 
  # representing non-annotated genes.
  subset_cordf <- cor_df |> 
  filter(target %in% genes) |> 
    dplyr::select(target, all_of(genes))
  
  # The subset is converted to a matrix-like data frame
  # and rownames are added.
  cor_mat <- subset_cordf[,-1]
  row.names(cor_mat) <- subset_cordf[,1]
  
  # Sorting the correlation matrix. This should place
  # 1 on the diagonal. Convert to matrix.
  cor_mat <- cor_mat[,rownames(cor_mat)]
  cor_mat <- as.matrix(cor_mat)
  # Check diagonal 
  # diag(cor_mat)
  
  # Regularize the correlation matrix
  cor_mat2 <- corpcor::cor.shrink(cor_mat)
  
  # Convert to distances and do clusters
  d <- as.dist(1 - abs(cor_mat2))
  
  hc <- hclust(d, method = "ward.D2")
  clusters <- cutree(hc, k = 6)
  
  # Save clusters for plotting
  clusters_df <- data.frame(label = names(clusters), 
           cluster = clusters, 
           row.names = NULL)
  
  # Plot A -- The dendogram plot 
  hcdat <- dendro_data(hc)

  hcdat$labels <- hcdat$labels |> 
    inner_join(clusters_df) |> 
    mutate(label = fct_reorder(label, cluster))
  
 pa <- ggplot() +
    geom_segment(data = segment(hcdat), 
               aes(x = y, y = x, xend = yend, yend = xend)) +
  #  geom_text(data = label(hcdat), 
  #          aes(x = x, y = y, label = label, hjust = 0, color = as.factor(cluster)), 
  #          size = 3) +
    geom_point(data = label(hcdat), 
               aes(x = y, y = x, color = as.factor(cluster) )) +
    

  scale_x_reverse(expand = c(0.2, 0)) + 
    theme(axis.text.x = element_blank(), 
          axis.ticks.x = element_blank(), 
          axis.title.x = element_blank(), 
          legend.position = "none")
  
  # Plot B --- Gene set scores
  
  # Find the highest scoring gene sets per cluster
  ids <- go_annotation |> 
      inner_join(clusters_df |> 
               dplyr::rename(target = label)) |> 
      summarise(.by = c(cluster, ID, Description), 
            m = mean(NES, na.rm = TRUE), 
            s = sd(NES, na.rm = TRUE), 
            es = m/s)  |> 
    # Filter NA in effect size (no standard deviations or mean normalized effect)
    filter(!is.na(es)) |> 
    # Get top N per cluster
    slice_max(order_by = es, by = cluster, n = 2) |> 
    mutate(ID = fct_reorder(ID, cluster)) |> 
    pull(ID)
    

 pb <-  go_annotation |> 
      inner_join(clusters_df |> 
               dplyr::rename(target = label)) |> 
         filter(ID %in% ids) |> 

    inner_join(hcdat$labels |> 
                 dplyr::rename(target = label)) |> 
    mutate(NES = if_else(NES < 0, NES, 
                         if_else(is.na(NES), min(NES), NES))) |> 
    dplyr::select(ID, NES, x, y, cluster) |> 
    pivot_wider(names_from = ID, 
                values_from = NES) |> 
    pivot_longer(names_to = "ID", values_to = "NES", cols = starts_with("GO")) |> 
    mutate(NES = if_else(is.na(NES), 0, NES)) |> 
        mutate(ID = factor(ID, levels = levels(ids))) |> 

    ggplot(aes(y = x, x = ID)) + geom_tile(aes(fill = NES)) + 
    theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1), 
          axis.text.y = element_blank(), 
          axis.title.y = element_blank(), 
          axis.ticks.y = element_blank())

     
 
 
 cowplot::plot_grid(pa, pb, align = "h")
 
  
  
}
```

<!-- Original write-up (superseded by the Results section below; it still cites foam cell differentiation and DNA replication, which did not survive the sample-mapping fix, so it is commented out rather than rendered)
Comparing gene-expression profiles between age groups at baseline (Young - Old) revealed marked differences, with `r n_diff_expressed` genes showing robust differences between the groups (FDR < 5%, @fig-age-diff A). Rank-based gene-set enrichment analysis [@xu2024a] indicated that young participants had relatively higher expression of genes related to aerobic energy metabolism (e.g., oxidative phosphorylation and mitochondrial gene expression) and relatively lower expression of genes related to immune system activation (humoral immune response and macrophage-derived foam cell differentiation) and RNA processing and DNA replication (e.g., regulation of alternative mRNA splicing, via spliceosome and nuclear DNA replication; @fig-age-diff B).
-->

#### Training effects

Next up we explore the training effect. First, the goal is to see which of the 7 training contrasts shows the strongest overall signal (most genes at FDR <5%, largest typical effect sizes), then we can decide where to focus the deeper GSEA work. Here we'll be running tests on age difference in training response (e.g., young_old_t3 contrast) and age difference in volume-dependent training response (young_old_volume_t3 contrast), and the main effects (young_t3, old_t3).

```{r}

# Isolating contrast terms to get a sense of how many genes are significant for each

training_contrasts <- m2s$summaries |> 
  dplyr::filter(term %in% c("young_t3", "old_t3", "young_old_t3", 
                             "mod_low_t3", "young_volume_t3", 
                             "old_volume_t3", "young_old_volume_t3"))


# FDR-correct within each contrast separately (each term is its own family of 16,878 tests)
training_contrasts <- training_contrasts |> 
  dplyr::mutate(p.adj = p.adjust(p.value, method = "BH"), .by = term)


# Quick summary: how many genes are significant per contrast?
training_contrasts |> 
  dplyr::summarise(.by = term,
                   n_sig_5pct = sum(p.adj < 0.05, na.rm = TRUE),
                   n_sig_1pct = sum(p.adj < 0.01, na.rm = TRUE),
                   median_abs_estimate = median(abs(estimate), na.rm = TRUE))



```

Both young (young_t3) and old (old_t3) show massive training effects: 3,503 and 4,241 genes at FDR <5% respectively (roughly 20-25% of the whole filtered transcriptome), i.e., training from baseline to post (t3) produces a large, broad transcriptional response in both age groups. Old shows slightly more genes and a somewhat smaller typical effect size (median |estimate| 0.061 vs. 0.075).

The young_old_t3 (overall training response diff by age) is essentially null, 1 gene at 5% and 0 at 1%. With the huge main effect in each group, this near null interaction suggests the magnitude/direction of the transcriptional training response is broadly similar between young and old, even though each group responds strongly on its own, they're not responding differently from each other in a significant genome-wide way. (This is a difference-of-differences test with lower power than the within-group tests, so "no significant difference" is not the same as "identical".)

Old_volume_t3 = 1216 genes at FDR <5%, 114 at FDR <1%. This tells us that within the old group, moderate vs. low volume produces a real, detectable difference in gene expression at post - meaningful on its own. For the young, this same effect (young_volume_t3) is essentially null (1 gene), which probably explains why the overall volume effect (averaged over age, mod_low_t3) is weak, with 143 genes at 5% and 5 at 1%. The young_old_volume_t3 is completely null (0 genes at both thresholds).

So put together, this shows that training produces a robust transcriptional response in both age groups, but a volume effect is detectable only in the old group (the formal young vs. old comparison of the volume effect is null, so this is "detectable in old, not in young" rather than a demonstrated difference). 

Since young_t3/old_t3 are the strongest and broadest signals, its the natural starting point for GSEA asking "what biological processes change with training in each age group". The old_volume_t3 is also quite interesting, asking "what's different about moderate vs. low volume specifically in the old".

#### Training effects fig

```{r}

# Finding the correct threshold of labelled genes

# a threshold of 20 (just a starting point) resulted in 144 genes for young and 221 for old, which would make the volcano basically unreadable

# Specific threshold testing

thresholds <- c(30, 35, 40, 45, 50, 55, 60)

purrr::map_dfr(thresholds, function(t) {
  young_n <- m2s$summaries |> 
    dplyr::filter(term == "young_t3") |> 
    dplyr::mutate(neglog2p = -log2(p.adjust(p.value, method = "BH"))) |> 
    dplyr::filter(neglog2p > t) |> 
    nrow()
  
  old_n <- m2s$summaries |> 
    dplyr::filter(term == "old_t3") |> 
    dplyr::mutate(neglog2p = -log2(p.adjust(p.value, method = "BH"))) |> 
    dplyr::filter(neglog2p > t) |> 
    nrow()
  
  data.frame(threshold = t, young_n = young_n, old_n = old_n)
})

# 40 seems like a sweet spot = 8 genes for young and 18 for old. This asymmetry is a genuine reflection of the larger gene-count in old (4241 vs. 3503). 

```

These volcano plots actually corroborate the GSEA results quite well. Almost every labelled gene in both panels is a collagen/ECM/basement-membrane gene (COL4A1, COL4A2, LAMB1, LAMA4, COL5A2, COL3A1, COL1A2, COL6A3, NID2, SPARC, PXDN), fitting the "training up-regulates ECM/connective tissue remodelling" pattern from the GSEA top-10 tables. Notably, the plot for old individuals shows a slightly more varied set beyond pure ECM, but this is still consistent with the old_t3's secondary coagulation/vascular theme - PECAM1 is a classic vascular/platelet endothelial marker, fitting the "regulation of coagulation"/"cellular extravasation" GO hits found only in old.

```{r}
#| label: fig-training-volcano
#| fig-cap: "Training effect (baseline to t3) in young and old participants. Volcano plots of the age-specific training contrasts (young_t3, old_t3); genes above the dashed line change at FDR < 5%, positive estimates indicate higher expression at t3. Genes with -log2(FDR) > 40 are labelled."

# Volcano Plots

p1_young <- m2s$summaries |> 
  filter(term == "young_t3") |> 
  separate_wider_regex(
    target,
    patterns = c(
      ensembl  = "ENSG\\d+",
      "\\.",
      version  = "[^_]+",      
      "_",
      symbol   = ".+"
    )
  ) |> 
  mutate(log2estimate = estimate / log(2), 
         p.value = p.adjust(p.value, method = "BH"), 
         flag = if_else(-log2(p.value) > 40, symbol, "")) |> 
  ggplot(aes(log2estimate, -log2(p.value)))  + 
  geom_hline(yintercept = -log2(0.05), lty = 2, color = "gray") +
  annotate("text", x = min(-2, na.rm=TRUE), y = -log2(0.05) + 1.5, 
           label = "FDR 5%", size = 3, hjust = 0, color = "gray") +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.3, color = "#0173B2") + 
  ggrepel::geom_text_repel(aes(label = flag), size = 3, 
                            max.overlaps = Inf, min.segment.length = 0) +   
  theme_classic() + 
  labs(x = "Estimate (log<sub>2</sub> change, baseline to t3)", 
       y = "log<sub>2</sub>(FDR)",
       title = "Young") + 
  theme(axis.title.x = ggtext::element_markdown(),
        axis.title.y = ggtext::element_markdown()) + 
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 85), expand = c(0,0))   

p1_old <- m2s$summaries |> 
  filter(term == "old_t3") |> 
  separate_wider_regex(
    target,
    patterns = c(
      ensembl  = "ENSG\\d+",
      "\\.",
      version  = "[^_]+",      
      "_",
      symbol   = ".+"
    )
  ) |> 
  mutate(log2estimate = estimate / log(2), 
         p.value = p.adjust(p.value, method = "BH"), 
         flag = if_else(-log2(p.value) > 40, symbol, "")) |> 
  ggplot(aes(log2estimate, -log2(p.value)))  + 
  geom_hline(yintercept = -log2(0.05), lty = 2, color = "gray") +
  annotate("text", x = min(-2, na.rm=TRUE), y = -log2(0.05) + 1.5, 
           label = "FDR 5%", size = 3, hjust = 0, color = "gray") +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.3, color = "#0173B2") + 
  ggrepel::geom_text_repel(aes(label = flag), size = 3, 
                            max.overlaps = Inf, min.segment.length = 0) +   
  theme_classic() + 
  labs(x = "Estimate (log<sub>2</sub> change, baseline to t3)", 
       y = "log<sub>2</sub>(FDR)",
       title = "Old") + 
  theme(axis.title.x = ggtext::element_markdown(),
        axis.title.y = ggtext::element_markdown()) + 
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 85), expand = c(0,0))   


# Side-by-side
cowplot::plot_grid(p1_young, p1_old, ncol = 2)

# Stacked alternative (more room for the labels in the old panel):
#cowplot::plot_grid(p1_young, p1_old, ncol = 1)


```

#### Results

Comparing gene-expression profiles between age groups at baseline (Young - Old) revealed marked differences, with `r n_diff_expressed` genes showing robust differences between the groups (FDR < 5%, @fig-age-diff A). Rank-based gene-set enrichment analysis [@xu2024a] indicated that young participants had relatively higher expression of genes related to aerobic energy metabolism (e.g., oxidative phosphorylation and mitochondrial gene expression) and relatively lower expression of genes related to immune system activation (e.g., complement activation and humoral immune response) and epigenetic regulation of gene expression (e.g., heterochromatin formation and regulation of alternative mRNA splicing, via spliceosome; @fig-age-diff B)

Training induced a large, broad transcriptional response in both age groups: `r n_sig_young_t3` genes changed from baseline to t3 in young participants, and `r n_sig_old_t3` in old participants (FDR < 5%, @fig-training-volcano). Individual genes with the strongest training-induced changes were predominantly collagen and basement-membrane genes in both groups (e.g., COL4A1, COL4A2, LAMB1, PXDN in young; COL4A1, LAMA4, COL3A1, COL1A2, SPARC in old; @fig-training-volcano), consistent with an extracellular matrix (ECM) remodeling response to resistance training.

Rank-based gene-set enrichment analysis [@xu2024a] showed that the dominant biology of the training response was remarkably similar between age groups: 6 of the top 10 enriched categories were shared, with matching direction and comparable magnitude in both young and old (RNA splicing, ribonucleoprotein complex biogenesis, integrin-mediated signaling pathway, cell adhesion mediated by integrin, collagen metabolic process, and mRNA transport; @fig-training-gsea). Training up-regulated genes related to ECM/connective tissue remodeling (e.g., integrin-mediated signaling and adhesion, collagen metabolic process) and down-regulated genes related to RNA-processing and ribosome biogenesis (e.g., RNA splicing, ribonucleoprotein complex biogenesis, mRNA transport) in both groups. <!--This similarity in the transcriptional training response was consistent with the age × time interaction contrast showing essentially no significant genes, indicating that the near-null interaction reflects genuinely similar biology between age groups rather than a lack of statistical power.--> A smaller set of categories differed by age: young participants showed additional enrichment for cytoplasmic translation, mesenchymal cell migration, and angiogenesis, while old participants showed additional enrichment for coagulation- and vascular-related categories. <!--(regulation of coagulation, cellular extravasation, regulation of blood coagulation) — reflected in old participants' volcano plot by genes such as PECAM1, a canonical vascular/platelet-endothelial marker (@fig-training-volcano).-->

In contrast to the broadly age-independent training effect, the effect of training volume (moderate vs. low) was age-dependent: a substantial number of genes differed by volume in old participants (`r n_sig_old_volume_t3` genes, FDR < 5%), while essentially no genes showed a volume effect in young participants. Among old participants, higher training volume was associated with relatively higher expression of genes related to mitochondrial biogenesis and oxidative metabolism (e.g., inner mitochondrial membrane organization, respiratory electron transport chain, purine-containing compound biosynthesis) and relatively lower expression of genes related to muscle contractile function and translation (e.g., skeletal muscle contraction, cytoplasmic translation, muscle organ development, striated muscle cell differentiation, ribosomal small subunit biogenesis). This volume effect was considerably more modest than the main training effect, both in the number of genes involved and in statistical strength. <!--(FDR values several orders of magnitude weaker than the training-effect contrasts).-->

## Ribosome biogenesis

Ribosome biogenesis (RiBi) is central to the thesis (UBF, c-Myc, total RNA), so we look at it specifically in the RNA-seq data. The analysis has four parts: (1) a targeted GSEA on a-priori RiBi gene sets, (2) the individual RiBi genes (Pol I machinery, processing and assembly factors, MYC), (3) a check of whether any RiBi signal is specific or just follows the general shift in myofibre transcripts (tissue composition), and (4) a record of a recentring approach that turned out to be invalid.

All analyses reuse the contrast tables from the GSEA sections above (`gsearesults*`), so no models are refitted. Requires clusterProfiler, org.Hs.eg.db and GO.db (loaded earlier / called with `::`).

### Targeted GSEA on RiBi gene sets

The genome-wide GSEA stores only terms with adjusted p < 0.01 (`pvalueCutoff = 0.01`), so a term that is missing from those tables is not necessarily unchanged. For an a-priori set of RiBi terms we therefore rerun GSEA on the stored ranked lists with `pvalueCutoff = 1`, restricted to the RiBi terms. BH adjustment is then over these few sets only, which is defensible because they were chosen in advance, but must be stated when reporting.

```{r}
#| label: ribi-gsea
#| code-fold: true
#| message: false
#| warning: false

# Contrast results collected in one list. Each element is the output of
# gsea_fun(): $gene_list (all genes with estimate, std.error, statistic,
# BH-adjusted p.value), $diff_genes_out, $gse_results, $gse_results_filtered.
# Contrast definitions (from sum_fun_contr):
#   baseline_age = young - old at baseline
#   young_t3 / old_t3 = t3 - baseline within age group (averaged over volume)
#   old_vol_t3 = moderate - low volume at t3 within old
#   young_vs_old = young_t3 - old_t3 (interaction)
gsea_list <- list(
  baseline_age = gsearesults,
  young_t3     = gsearesults_young_t3,
  old_t3       = gsearesults_old_t3,
  old_vol_t3   = gsearesults_old_volume_t3,
  young_vs_old = gsearesults_young_old_t3
)

# A-priori RiBi terms (GO biological process). Descendant terms are included
# via the GOALL mapping below, so these are the full sets.
ribi_go <- c(
  "ribosome biogenesis"                  = "GO:0042254",
  "ribosomal large subunit biogenesis"   = "GO:0042273",
  "ribosomal small subunit biogenesis"   = "GO:0042274",
  "rRNA processing"                      = "GO:0006364",
  "maturation of SSU-rRNA"               = "GO:0030490",
  "transcription by RNA polymerase I"    = "GO:0006360",
  "ncRNA processing"                     = "GO:0034470",
  "ribonucleoprotein complex biogenesis" = "GO:0022613",  # overlaps heavily with splicing genes
  "rRNA metabolic process"               = "GO:0016072"
)

# TERM2GENE table: all genes annotated to each term, incl. descendant terms.
term2gene <- AnnotationDbi::select(org.Hs.eg.db,
                                   keys = unname(ribi_go),
                                   keytype = "GOALL", columns = "ENSEMBL") |>
  dplyr::distinct(GOALL, ENSEMBL) |>
  tidyr::drop_na() |>
  dplyr::rename(term = GOALL, gene = ENSEMBL)

# GSEA on one contrast, using the same ranking statistic as gsea_fun().
# maxGSSize is raised to 1000 (genome-wide run used 500) because the broad terms
# are large. NOTE: this returns 8 of the 9 terms; ncRNA processing is presumably
# dropped for exceeding maxGSSize.
run_ribi_gsea <- function(x) {
  gl <- setNames(x$gene_list$statistic, x$gene_list$ensembl) |>
    sort(decreasing = TRUE)
  GSEA(gl, TERM2GENE = term2gene,
       minGSSize = 15, maxGSSize = 1000,
       pvalueCutoff = 1,      # keep all terms, not only significant ones
       eps = 0, nPermSimple = 10000, verbose = FALSE) |>
    as.data.frame()
}

ribi_gsea <- purrr::imap_dfr(gsea_list, \(x, nm)
    run_ribi_gsea(x) |> dplyr::mutate(contrast = nm)) |>
  dplyr::mutate(Description = unname(
    AnnotationDbi::mapIds(GO.db::GO.db, ID, "TERM", "GOID"))) |>
  dplyr::select(contrast, ID, Description, setSize, NES, pvalue, p.adjust) |>
  dplyr::arrange(contrast, p.adjust)

ribi_gsea
```

### Individual RiBi genes

Gene sets can hide which genes drive a signal, and the GO term "ribonucleoprotein complex biogenesis" overlaps strongly with the splicing machinery. We therefore look at a short a-priori list of genes: the Pol I machinery and upstream drivers (`UBTF`, `RRN3`, `POLR1*`, `TAF1*`, `MYC`) and processing/assembly factors (snoRNP: `FBL`, `NOP56`, `NOP58`, `DKC1`; PeBoW: `PES1`, `BOP1`, `WDR12`; UTP-A: `WDR43`; `NPM1`, `NCL`). Estimates are on the natural-log scale and converted to % change. Intervals are Wald-type from m2, unadjusted for multiplicity across genes, so they are descriptive.

```{r}
#| label: fig-ribi-genes
#| code-fold: true
#| fig-cap: "Percent change in expression of individual ribosome biogenesis genes (point and 95% Wald interval from m2). young_t3 and old_t3: t3 vs. baseline. old_vol_t3: moderate vs. low volume at t3 in the old group."

ribi_genes <- c(
  # Pol I machinery and upstream drivers
  "UBTF","RRN3","POLR1A","POLR1B","POLR1E","TAF1A","TAF1B","TAF1C","TAF1D","MYC",
  # Processing and assembly factors
  "FBL","DKC1","NOP56","NOP58","NPM1","NCL","PES1","BOP1","WDR12","WDR43")

ribi_tab <- purrr::imap_dfr(gsea_list, \(x, nm)
  x$gene_list |>
    dplyr::filter(symbol %in% ribi_genes) |>
    dplyr::mutate(contrast = nm))

# Any genes removed by the expression filter?
setdiff(ribi_genes, ribi_tab$symbol)

ribi_tab |>
  dplyr::filter(contrast %in% c("young_t3", "old_t3", "old_vol_t3")) |>
  dplyr::mutate(pct = 100 * (exp(estimate) - 1),
                lo  = 100 * (exp(estimate - 1.96 * std.error) - 1),
                hi  = 100 * (exp(estimate + 1.96 * std.error) - 1)) |>
  ggplot(aes(pct, reorder(symbol, pct), colour = contrast)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = 2) +
  geom_pointrange(aes(xmin = lo, xmax = hi), position = position_dodge(width = 0.6)) +
  labs(x = "% change (t3 vs. baseline; moderate vs. low for old_vol_t3)", y = NULL)
```

### Is the RiBi signal specific, or does it follow myofibre content?

After training, the strongest positive GSEA terms are extracellular matrix, collagen and angiogenesis (non-myofibre transcripts), and the myofibre-specific "skeletal muscle contraction" term falls. This raises the possibility that part of the RiBi (and splicing/translation) decrease reflects a change in tissue composition of the biopsy, not RiBi regulation. Three descriptive checks:

1. Transcriptome-wide median shift per contrast (is the data well centred?), compared with the median shift of myofibre genes and of ribosomal protein genes.
2. Expression of marker genes for non-myofibre cell types (fibroblast, endothelial, immune, satellite cell).
3. A direct comparison of the median change in the RiBi set with the median change in myofibre genes, with a bootstrap interval for the difference.

```{r}
#| label: ribi-composition
#| code-fold: true

# --- 1. Median shifts ------------------------------------------------------
# Probe set used in the first pass (9 genes, incl. fibre-type genes, which can
# change with training for real). A wider contractile set is used in step 3.
probe_9 <- c("ACTA1","CKM","DES","MYH1","MYH2","MYH7","TNNT1","TNNT3","MB")

purrr::imap_dfr(gsea_list, \(x, nm) {
  g <- x$gene_list
  tibble::tibble(
    contrast       = nm,
    median_all     = 100 * (exp(median(g$estimate)) - 1),
    median_probe   = 100 * (exp(median(g$estimate[g$symbol %in% probe_9])) - 1),
    median_RPL_RPS = 100 * (exp(median(g$estimate[grepl("^RP[LS]\\d", g$symbol)])) - 1))
})

# --- 2. Non-myofibre cell-type markers --------------------------------------
# Result: COL1A1, PECAM1 and PTPRC rise by roughly 30-110% after training in
# both age groups (see summary); PAX7 is higher in young at baseline.
markers <- c(fibroblast = "COL1A1", fibroblast2 = "PDGFRA", endothelial = "PECAM1",
             endothelial2 = "VWF", immune = "PTPRC", satellite = "PAX7")

purrr::imap_dfr(gsea_list, \(x, nm)
  x$gene_list |>
    dplyr::filter(symbol %in% markers) |>
    dplyr::mutate(contrast = nm, pct = 100 * (exp(estimate) - 1))) |>
  dplyr::select(contrast, symbol, pct, p.value)

# --- 3. RiBi set vs. myofibre genes, with bootstrap interval ----------------
# RiBi = all genes annotated to GO:0042254 (ribosome biogenesis).
ribi_ens <- unique(term2gene$gene[term2gene$term == "GO:0042254"])

# Two reference sets: a broad contractile set (incl. fibre-type genes, which can
# change with training for real) and a pan-fibre set without them.
probe_sets <- list(
  contractile13 = c("ACTA1","CKM","DES","MB","TNNT1","TNNT3","MYH1","MYH2","MYH7",
                    "TTN","NEB","MYBPC1","MYBPC2"),
  panfibre4     = c("ACTA1","CKM","DES","MB")
)
probe_contractile <- probe_sets$contractile13   # used in the abandoned chunk below

# Bootstrap resamples genes within each set and takes the difference in
# medians. Caveats: genes are treated as independent (they are not), so the
# interval is too narrow; with few probe genes the median is lumpy (very much so
# with 4), so intervals are wide and not always centred on the estimate.
set.seed(1)
ribi_vs_probe <- purrr::imap_dfr(probe_sets, \(probe, pname)
  purrr::imap_dfr(gsea_list[c("young_t3", "old_t3", "old_vol_t3")], \(x, nm) {
    g <- x$gene_list
    r <- g$estimate[g$ensembl %in% ribi_ens]
    p <- g$estimate[g$symbol %in% probe]
    d <- replicate(5000, median(sample(r, replace = TRUE)) -
                         median(sample(p, replace = TRUE)))
    tibble::tibble(
      probe_set = pname, contrast = nm,
      ribi_pct  = 100 * (exp(median(r)) - 1),
      probe_pct = 100 * (exp(median(p)) - 1),
      diff_pct  = 100 * (exp(median(r) - median(p)) - 1),
      lo = 100 * (exp(quantile(d, 0.025)) - 1),
      hi = 100 * (exp(quantile(d, 0.975)) - 1))
  }))

ribi_vs_probe
```

### Abandoned approach: recentred GSEA

We tried to remove the myofibre shift by subtracting the median log fold change of the probe genes from every gene and rerunning GSEA. **This is not valid and its results must not be interpreted.** Subtracting a constant does not change the ranking; GSEA responds only through the score weights, and after the shift almost all statistics are of one sign, so fgsea cannot compute p-values for several terms (terms silently dropped for `young_t3` and `old_t3`). The z-based version (`(estimate - shift) / std.error`) is biased the other way: it boosts precisely measured, highly expressed genes, which favours RiBi and ribosomal sets. The code is kept for the record only (`eval: false`). A proper fix would be a composition covariate in the model itself.

```{r}
#| label: ribi-recentred-abandoned
#| eval: false

refs <- list(
  none        = character(0),
  panfibre    = c("ACTA1","CKM","DES","MB"),
  contractile = probe_contractile
)

run_rc <- function(g, ref, use_z = TRUE) {
  shift <- if (length(ref)) median(g$estimate[g$symbol %in% ref]) else 0
  stat  <- if (use_z) (g$estimate - shift) / g$std.error else (g$estimate - shift)
  gl    <- setNames(stat, g$ensembl) |> sort(decreasing = TRUE)
  GSEA(gl, TERM2GENE = term2gene, minGSSize = 15, maxGSSize = 1000,
       pvalueCutoff = 1, eps = 0, nPermSimple = 10000, verbose = FALSE) |>
    as.data.frame() |>
    dplyr::mutate(shift_pct = 100 * (exp(shift) - 1), n_terms = dplyr::n())
}

# z-based (biased towards highly expressed genes) and estimate-based
# (ranking unchanged; unbalanced list) versions:
# sens     <- purrr::imap_dfr(refs, \(ref, rn) purrr::imap_dfr(gsea_list[c("old_t3","young_t3","old_vol_t3")],
#               \(x, nm) run_rc(x$gene_list, ref) |> dplyr::mutate(ref = rn, contrast = nm)))
# sens_lfc <- same call with run_rc(..., use_z = FALSE)
```

### Summary of findings: ribosome biogenesis

**Targeted GSEA** (eight RiBi terms; BH over these sets only)

- Baseline (young vs. old): no RiBi term is significant (best p.adjust 0.08). Terms lean positive, Pol I transcription leans the other way.
- Training effect (t3 vs. baseline): all eight terms are negative in both age groups, e.g. ribosome biogenesis NES −2.59 (old) and −2.66 (young), p.adjust about 1e-23 and 1e-28. The weakest terms (large-subunit biogenesis, Pol I transcription) are still significant (p.adjust ≤ 1e-3).
- Moderate vs. low volume in old: also negative (ribosome biogenesis NES −1.64, p.adjust 2e-5).
- Age interaction (young change minus old change): negative, i.e. the decrease is larger in young (ribosome biogenesis NES −1.85, p.adjust 2e-8; Pol I transcription not significant, p.adjust 0.063).
- The eight terms are nested and overlap heavily, so they are one signal, not eight findings. "Ribonucleoprotein complex biogenesis" also overlaps with the splicing machinery, which is strongly negative in the same contrasts.

**Individual genes** (@fig-ribi-genes, values read from the plot, approximate)

- Pol I initiation machinery and drivers (`UBTF`, `RRN3`, `POLR1A/B/E`, `TAF1A–D`, `MYC`): small changes, mostly within ±10% with intervals spanning zero. `MYC`, `TAF1A` and `TAF1B` are, if anything, higher in the old group (about +11 to +12%, wide intervals).
- Processing and assembly factors (`BOP1`, `FBL`, `NOP58`, `WDR43`, `NCL`, `PES1`, `DKC1`): clearer decreases of roughly 5–13% in at least one age group.
- Moderate vs. low volume in old: wide intervals and mixed directions, so the GSEA signal reflects small coordinated shifts and not standout genes.

**Is it RiBi-specific?** (descriptive checks)

- The transcriptome-wide median shift is within ±0.8% in every contrast, so the data are well centred.
- Myofibre probe genes (9-gene set) fall by about 5.5% (young t3), 9.2% (old t3) and 11.5% (moderate vs. low, old), and are 12.3% higher in young than old at baseline. Ribosomal protein genes fall by 7.0%, 4.2% and 5.9% in the same contrasts.
- RiBi (GO:0042254) median change vs. myofibre genes, with two reference sets (13 contractile genes; 4 pan-fibre genes without fibre-type genes):

| Contrast | RiBi | Myofibre (13) | Difference, 13 genes (95% interval) | Myofibre (4) | Difference, 4 genes (95% interval) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| young_t3 | −5.8% | −5.7% | −0.1% (−1.2 to +8.2) | −5.8% | 0.0% (−7.2 to +11.5) |
| old_t3 | −3.4% | −9.2% | +6.4% (−0.2 to +8.6) | −9.2% | +6.5% (−4.0 to +15.5) |
| old_vol_t3 | −0.6% | −9.0% | +9.2% (+3.1 to +17.8) | −13.6% | +15.1% (+6.6 to +19.6) |

- Young: RiBi falls exactly as much as the myofibre genes, so there is no evidence of a selective RiBi change. Old: RiBi falls less than the myofibre genes, but the interval touches zero. Moderate vs. low volume in old: myofibre genes fall by about 9–14% while RiBi is essentially unchanged; the interval excludes zero with both reference sets (+9% and +15%), so this does not depend on the fibre-type genes, but the size depends on which genes are used as reference. It is a hypothesis-level hint that moderate volume retains RiBi expression relative to myofibre content. This is compatible with the GSEA result for the same contrast: RiBi is slightly lower than the average gene (about 1%), but far higher than the myofibre genes.
- Non-myofibre marker genes (% change; adjusted p-values from the contrast tables, only partly inspected):

| Marker | Baseline (young vs. old) | young_t3 | old_t3 | old_vol_t3 | Interaction |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `COL1A1` (matrix/fibroblast) | +7.7 | +111 | +96 | +14.4 | +7.9 |
| `PECAM1` (endothelial; also leukocytes) | +5.7 | +31.1 | +29.9 | +15.2 | +0.9 |
| `PTPRC` (immune) | −10.4 | +33.3 | +34.7 | +26.2 | −1.0 |
| `PAX7` (satellite cell) | +23.8 | +15.2 | +19.0 | +1.9 | −3.2 |
| `VWF` (endothelial) | +5.8 | +8.5 | +4.5 | −2.1 | +3.8 |
| `PDGFRA` (fibro-adipogenic progenitor) | +5.8 | −2.5 | +8.4 | −3.9 | −10.1 |

  After training, `COL1A1`, `PECAM1` and `PTPRC` rise by about 30–110% in both age groups, similar in size in young and old, while the myofibre genes fall by about 5–9%. Moderate vs. low volume in old adds a further rise in `PTPRC` (+26%), `PECAM1` (+15%) and `COL1A1` (+14%), in line with the further drop in myofibre genes (about −9%). At baseline only `PAX7` differs (higher in young, adjusted p = 0.021). `PDGFRA` and `VWF` barely move, so the evidence for expansion of progenitor cells and of larger-vessel endothelium is weak; `PECAM1` is also expressed on leukocytes, so it overlaps with `PTPRC`. Significance for the `old_vol_t3` column was not inspected.
- The real median shifts are small (about 1–6%). GSEA p-values reflect consistency across hundreds of genes, not effect size, and should be reported together with magnitudes.

**Interpretation and caveats**

- The RiBi transcript decrease after training cannot be separated from a general decrease in myofibre-abundant transcripts, which fits a change in biopsy composition (more extracellular matrix, immune and endothelial content, and likely satellite cells; training-related remodelling is plausible biology, not a technical artefact). The marker genes support this directly, but single markers are imperfect proxies and this is not a formal deconvolution. The composition shift is similar in size in young and old. There is no support for a selective Myc-driven change in RiBi transcription.
- The age difference in the response is the most robust remaining signal; probe genes show almost no age difference in response (+0.9%), so the composition shift does not obviously explain it, but this was not tested formally.
- The comparison depends on the probe genes being a fair reference (fibre-type genes may change for real; a pan-fibre-only set gave the same result), treats genes as independent, and uses a 13-gene set. The recentred GSEA is invalid and is not evidence either way.
- Not yet done: discuss a composition covariate in the model with Daniel. Biopsy timing relative to the last session and the library prep (poly-A vs. rRNA depletion) also affect how mRNA-level RiBi results should be read, and mRNA of RiBi factors is only an indirect readout compared with total RNA per mg and UBF/c-Myc protein.
